tagline: River wetlands connect Meskwaki country, Lincoln Highway landmarks and Amana villages.
intro: The Iowa Valley Scenic Byway follows 77 paved miles through agricultural country and Iowa River wetlands. Travel Iowa presents the route through its farmland, river habitat and cultural communities, from the edge of the Meskwaki Settlement to the Amana Colonies. Near Chelsea, the floodplain lies among partially wooded hills; northwest of town, an observation deck takes the shape of an eagle in flight. The Iowa River Corridor is also a focus area for conservation and preservation.

An earlier road left visible marks in two of the byway’s towns. In Tama, local Lincoln Highway boosters paid for concrete railings bearing the road’s name on a bridge built in 1914. When the Lincoln Highway was rerouted through Belle Plaine, a gas station moved in 1921 to capture its traffic. That station became Preston’s, where antique advertising and highway signs now cover the former station and garage.

Travel east from the Meskwaki Settlement’s edge through Tama, Chelsea and Belle Plaine, then continue toward Marengo and the Amana villages. Most of the settlement is private; the Meskwaki Cultural Center & Museum offers exhibits on tribal history. Farther east, Marengo has a Carnegie library and the Iowa County Courthouse. At Amana, the Heritage Museum introduces the communal kitchens, church and blacksmith shop.

moments.title: Lincoln Highway Bridge, Tama
moments.text: The words “Lincoln Highway” form part of the concrete railings on Tama’s bridge over Mud Creek. Local boosters paid for those railings to promote the road, turning a creek crossing into an advertisement for the route itself. The Iowa Highway Commission designed the bridge, and Strawberry Point contractor Paul N. Kingsley built it in 1914. The span measures 22 feet across, with a width of 24 feet. Its railings rise 3.33 feet, carrying the highway’s name above the creek. The bridge was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.
moments.notice: The highway’s name is formed in the bridge’s concrete railings.

moments.title: Preston's Station, Belle Plaine
moments.text: Preston’s Station moved to meet the motorists. Built in 1912, the gas station shifted to Fourth Avenue in 1921 when the Lincoln Highway was rerouted through Belle Plaine. George W. Preston bought it two years later for $100. A concrete block garage joined it in 1943, serving automobile repairs before housing Preston’s memorabilia. The garage retains a sliding barn door on its front, and a three-unit motel joined the property before 1949. Gas sales ended in 1989. Antique advertising and highway signs now cover both buildings, and the collection occupies the former gas station as well.
moments.notice: Antique advertising and highway signs cover the former station and its neighboring garage.

moments.title: Amana Colonies
moments.text: Communal life ended in the seven Amana villages in 1932, but the land was not divided into individual holdings. The German Radical Pietists who built the colonies had farmed and practiced specialized crafts within a communal economy. During the Great Depression, the community separated its religious organization from a joint-stock business, completing the change in 1932. More than 450 buildings from the communal period remain in the villages. The Community of True Inspiration continues to worship in Middle Amana. The Amana Heritage Museum directs visitors to a communal kitchen, the church and a blacksmith shop.
moments.notice: In July, thousands of American lotus flowers bloom on Lily Lake at Amana.
